title: Signals and Systems, MIT 6.003, Fall 2011
topics: Session 9 — Frequency Response, review and motivation (Lecture 9, slides 2-12): convolution and impulse responses, microscope point-spread functions, Hubble optical blur, audio equalization, and a mass-spring-dashpot demonstration.

Session 9 — Eigenfunctions and rational system functions (Lecture 9, slides 13-18): eigenfunction/eigenvalue definitions, complex exponentials as LTI eigenfunctions, and polynomial-ratio system functions.
Session 9 — Pole-zero vector diagrams (Lecture 9, slides 19-21 and 26-56): graphical evaluation of magnitude and phase from distances and angles to poles and zeros.
Session 9 — Sinusoidal frequency response (Lecture 9, slides 22-25): conjugate symmetry and the amplitude/phase response obtained by evaluating H(s) on the j-omega axis.
Session 9 — Second-order resonance (Lecture 9, slides 49-67): mass-spring-dashpot transfer function, resonant-frequency geometry, and the frequency of minus-pi/2 phase.

Session 10 — Perching UAV case study (Lecture 10, slides 2-14): biological motivation, dimensionless drag analysis, experiment design, motion capture, real-flight system identification, trajectory results, and flow visualization.
Session 10 — Feedback-control structure (Lecture 10, slides 15-20): plant, sensor, controller, error signal, and the discrete-time wallFinder model.
Session 10 — wallFinder without sensor delay (Lecture 10, slides 21-29): closed-loop system function, pole placement, monotonic/alternating/divergent regimes, and one-step convergence.

Session 10 — wallFinder with sensor delay (Lecture 10, slides 30-53): delayed feedback model, second-order pole locus, oscillation period, fastest achievable response, and degradation with added delay.
Session 11 — Continuous-time frequency-response review (Lecture 11, slides 3-7): complex-exponential eigenfunctions, vector evaluation, and pole-zero descriptions.
Session 11 — Bode magnitude plots (Lecture 11, slides 8-21 and 31-38): isolated-pole/zero asymptotes, products becoming sums on log axes, break frequencies, decibels, slopes, and approximation error.
Session 11 — Bode phase plots (Lecture 11, slides 22-30 and 39-42): straight-line pole/zero phase contributions, additive phase, gain-sign ambiguity, and phase-plot matching.
Session 11 — High-Q second-order systems (Lecture 11, slides 43-63): resonant peak, peak gain, normalized 3 dB bandwidth, and rapid phase transition.
Session 12 — Op-amp performance model (Lecture 12, slides 3-14): ideal versus LM741 behavior, dominant pole, frequency response, and step-response time constant.
Session 12 — Op-amp feedback (Lecture 12, slides 13-24): closed-loop transfer function, pole movement, bandwidth/speed improvement, and the gain-bandwidth tradeoff.
Session 12 — DC motor position control (Lecture 12, slides 25-31): integrator plant, potentiometer feedback, proportional gain, pole location, and first-order step response.

Session 12 — Motor inertia and second-order limits (Lecture 12, slides 32-40): integrator-with-lag plant, root locus, pole collision, oscillation, and why increasing gain no longer guarantees faster convergence.
Session 13 — Robustness to parameter variation (Lecture 13, slides 3-8): power-amplifier gain variation and negative feedback's reduced sensitivity.
Session 13 — Crossover distortion (Lecture 13, slides 9-18): transistor dead zone, waveform distortion, gain-dependent feedback correction, and an audio demonstration.

Session 13 — Magnetic levitation (Lecture 13, slides 19-35): unstable positive feedback, force linearization, spring analogy, feedback-current control, marginal stability, and added-zero stabilization.
Session 13 — Inverted pendulum (Lecture 13, slides 36-40): nonlinear equation, small-angle linearization, unstable poles, and feedback stabilization.
Problem Set 5, Problems 1-3 with solutions: closed-form DT and CT convolutions and visual matching of finite-support convolution shapes.
Problem Set 5, Engineering Problem 4 with solution: the anti-causal left-shift operator L, two-sided impulse responses, rational operator forms, and pole interpretation.
Problem Set 5, Engineering Problem 5 with solution: upsampling an image by three, triangle-kernel convolution, separable bilinear interpolation, and comparison with pixel replication.
Problem Set 5, Engineering Problem 6 with solution: one- and two-dimensional matched filtering, binary template centering, smiley detection, and noise robustness.
Problem Set 6, Problems 1-2 with solutions: frequencies of maximum gain for related second-order systems and a minus-90-degree phase calculation by algebra and vectors.
Problem Set 6, Problems 3-4 with solutions: closed-loop pole ranges for stability and real-valued poles in analogous continuous- and discrete-time feedback systems.
Problem Set 6, Engineering Problem 5 with solution: automotive suspension modeling, undamped oscillation, critical damping, and overdamping that transmits road motion.

Problem Set 6, Engineering Problem 6 with solution: DTMF column detection using sampled resonators, pole angle/radius selection, difference-equation implementation, and discrimination-speed tradeoffs.
Problem Set 7, Problem 1 with solution: extracting decay time, period, and cycles-per-e-fold from continuous- and discrete-time second-order pole pairs.
Problem Set 7, Problem 2 with solution: matching six pole-zero diagrams to impulse responses, Bode magnitudes, and Bode phases.
Problem Set 7, Engineering Problem 3 with solution: root-locus analysis of the phase-shift oscillator behind Hewlett and Packard's founding patent.
Problem Set 7, Engineering Problem 4 with solution: proportional, derivative, and proportional-derivative steering controllers for a constant-speed car.
Quiz 2, Problem 1 with solution (15 points): deriving a constant-coefficient differential equation from the two-sided impulse response exp(-|t|).
Quiz 2, Problem 2 with solution (15 points): eliminating the internal signal from a continuous-time feedback loop.
Quiz 2, Problem 3 with solution (30 points): recognizing possible and impossible finite-sequence convolutions.
Quiz 2, Problem 4 with solution (20 points): poles and zeros of a feedback system whose impulse response is (1+t)u(t).
Quiz 2, Problem 5 with solution (20 points): straight-line magnitude and phase Bode plots for a feedback system.
key_results: Lecture 9, slides 13-17: a signal is an eigenfunction when the system output is a scalar multiple of it; every eternal complex exponential exp(st) is an eigenfunction of an LTI system, with eigenvalue H(s).

Lecture 9, slides 22-25: for a real LTI system H(-jomega)=H*(jomega), so input cos(omega0 t) produces |H(jomega0)| cos(omega0 t + angle H(jomega0)); frequency response is H(s) restricted to the j-omega axis.

Lecture 9, slides 19-21: for a rational H(s), magnitude at s0 is the gain times the product of distances from s0 to zeros divided by the product of distances to poles; phase is the gain angle plus zero-vector angles minus pole-vector angles.

Lecture 9, slides 57-61: for conjugate poles at -sigma +/- j omega_d, the resonant-frequency maximum occurs below omega_d, at omega^2=omega_d^2-sigma^2=omega_0^2-2sigma^2 when that quantity is positive.

Lecture 9, slides 62-67: the mass-spring-dashpot response has phase -pi/2 at the undamped natural frequency omega0=sqrt(K/M), even though its amplitude peak occurs at a lower frequency when damping is present.
Lecture 10, slides 18-24: wallFinder without sensor delay has closed-loop pole p0=1+KT; -1<KT<0 gives monotone convergence, -2<KT<-1 gives alternating convergence, and KT<-2 diverges.
Lecture 10, slides 22-29: KT=-1 puts the sole no-delay closed-loop pole at zero, giving a one-sample response and exact one-step arrival in the idealized robot model.

Lecture 10, slides 36-43: one sample of sensor delay changes the characteristic polynomial to z^2-z-KT and the poles to 1/2 +/- sqrt(1/4+KT); sufficiently negative gain creates complex poles and oscillation.

Lecture 10, slides 48-53: the fastest one-delay response occurs at the repeated pole z=1/2 when KT=-1/4; adding a second delay moves the fastest repeated pole to about 0.682, showing quantitatively that delay slows the best achievable control response.

Lecture 11, slides 15-31: factor a rational transfer function into pole/zero sections; on logarithmic coordinates, products of magnitude become sums, and phase contributions also add, which makes a Bode plot a section-by-section construction.

Lecture 11, slides 8-25 and 33-38: a first-order zero contributes a +20 dB/decade high-frequency slope and approaches +pi/2 phase; a first-order pole contributes -20 dB/decade and approaches -pi/2, with the break at the pole/zero magnitude.
Lecture 11, slides 33-38: magnitude in decibels is 20 log10 |H(jomega)|; the straight-line first-order approximation is exact asymptotically and misses by about 3 dB at the break frequency.

Lecture 11, slides 43-63: for the normalized high-Q second-order system, peak magnitude grows approximately as Q, normalized 3 dB bandwidth shrinks approximately as 1/Q, and phase changes by roughly pi/2 across that bandwidth.
Lecture 12, slides 6-14: the LM741 is modeled as K(s)=alpha K0/(s+alpha) with K0=2x10^5 and alpha=40 rad/s, giving a dominant-pole time constant of 1/40 s and a corner near 6.4 Hz.

Lecture 12, slides 13-23: negative feedback with factor beta changes the op-amp pole to -alpha(1+beta K0), shortens response time and widens bandwidth by 1+beta K0, but reduces DC gain to K0/(1+beta K0); feedback trades gain for speed/bandwidth rather than increasing the initial slew rate.

Lecture 12, slides 25-31: treating DC-motor angle as the integral of voltage, proportional position feedback yields a first-order closed-loop pole at -alpha beta gamma and a step response with final value 1/beta; increasing amplifier gain speeds this idealized model.

Lecture 12, slides 32-39: when motor inertia adds a lag pole, increasing proportional gain makes two real poles collide at -p/2 and then become a complex pair; convergence cannot be made arbitrarily fast by gain alone.
Lecture 13, slides 4-8: the uncertain power-amplifier loop has gain KF0/(1+beta KF0), which approaches 1/beta for large K and becomes nearly independent of both K and the varying plant factor F0.

Lecture 13, slides 9-17: high loop gain reduces the waveform error created by a push-pull transistor dead zone, so negative feedback can suppress a rapidly varying nonlinear distortion, not just static parameter error.

Lecture 13, slides 19-34: the linearized magnetic-levitation plant has poles +/-sqrt(K/M), including one right-half-plane pole; proportional current feedback can move them to the imaginary axis but leaves marginal stability.

Lecture 13, slide 35: adding a zero to the magnetic-levitation controller supplies the extra phase/damping needed to move the poles into the left half-plane and stabilize the plant for sufficient gain.
Lecture 13, slides 36-39: the linearized inverted pendulum has poles at +/-sqrt(g/l), hence one unstable natural mode, but cart-motion feedback can stabilize it.

Problem Set 5 Solution, Problems 1-2, pp. 1-6: convolving with a unit step computes a running sum in DT or running integral in CT; convolving identical exponential modes creates an additional n or t factor, reflecting a repeated pole.

Problem Set 5 Solution, Problem 4, pp. 7-8: left-shift operators express anti-causal recursions; the two-sided response (1/2)^|n| has poles at z=1/2 and z=2, with one causal and one anti-causal geometric component.

Problem Set 5 Solution, Problem 5, pp. 9-12: threefold linear interpolation is implemented by inserting two zeros between samples and convolving with a five-point triangle [1/3, 2/3, 1, 2/3, 1/3]; applying it separably in two dimensions gives bilinear interpolation.

Problem Set 5 Solution, Problem 6, pp. 13-15: centering binary pixels at +/-127.5 makes both black-black and white-white matches positive and mismatches negative, turning 2D convolution into an effective matched filter.

Problem Set 6 Solution, Problem 1, pp. 1-3: adding one and then two zeros at the origin to 1/(1+s+s^2) shifts the maximum-gain frequency from 1/sqrt(2) to 1 and then sqrt(2), because numerator weighting increasingly favors high frequency.

Problem Set 6 Solution, Problems 3-4, pp. 5-6: the analogous CT and DT feedback denominators share pole formulas but not stability regions: CT stability requires K>2, while DT stability requires 2<K<3 because DT poles must remain inside the unit circle.

Problem Set 6 Solution, Problem 5, pp. 7-9: for M=K=1, the suspension poles become real at B>=2; B=2 is the smallest nonoscillatory damping, while B=100 makes the impulse response nearly an impulse and transmits wheel motion directly to the car.

Problem Set 6 Solution, Problem 6, pp. 9-12: a sampled two-pole resonator detects a DTMF column by placing poles at r exp(+/-jOmega0), with Omega0 set by the target tone and r close enough to one for selectivity but below one for stability and adequate settling.

Problem Set 7 Solution, Problem 1, pp. 1-3: CT conjugate poles -sigma +/- j omega_d give decay time 1/sigma and period 2pi/omega_d; DT poles r0 exp(+/-jOmega0) give e-fold sample count -1/ln r0 and period 2pi/Omega0.

Problem Set 7 Solution, Problem 3, pp. 5-6: the three-section RC feedback oscillator reaches marginal stability at K=8; its period is 2pi RC/sqrt(3), so R=1 kohm and C=1 microfarad give 3.63 ms and increasing R tenfold gives 36.3 ms.

Problem Set 7 Solution, Problem 4, pp. 6-9: proportional-only steering is undamped, derivative-only steering leaves a position offset, and combined proportional-derivative feedback permits independently useful control of convergence rate and oscillation through omega0 and Q.

Quiz 2 Solution, Problem 1, p. 2: the two-sided impulse response exp(-|t|) has H(s)=2/(1-s^2), hence the LTI relation y(t)-y''(t)=2x(t); the example tests bilateral-transform reasoning rather than causal assumptions.
Quiz 2 Solution, Problem 4, p. 6: closing gain-4 negative feedback around g(t)=(1+t)u(t) converts G(s)=(s+1)/s^2 into H(s)=(s+1)/(s+2)^2, producing one zero at -1 and a repeated pole at -2.
pedagogy: This shard is taught as a fast loop between physical intuition, pole-zero geometry, algebra, and experiment. Lecture slides reveal constructions incrementally, often asking a multiple-choice 'Check Yourself' question before supplying a geometric or algebraic derivation. Frequency response begins with optical blur, audio, and a vibrating mass; feedback is motivated by an instrumented perching UAV, then reduced to wall-following, op-amp, motor, amplifier, levitation, and inverted-pendulum models. The slides repeatedly compare a schematic, its block diagram, its system function, its pole motion, and its time/frequency response. Problem Sets 5-7 contain 16 problems total: nine shorter analytic exercises and seven explicitly labeled Engineering Design Problems involving images, matched filters, suspensions, touch-tone decoding, oscillator history, and robotic steering; worked solutions expose reasoning and implementation code rather than only answers. Problem Set 7 is optional exam practice. Quiz 2 is a closed-book, five-problem, 100-point synthesis assessment covering differential equations, convolution, feedback, poles/zeros, and Bode plots. The shard assumes prior facility with convolution, Laplace/z transforms, causal LTI systems, and basic differential/difference equations, then emphasizes estimation, design choice, and stability over formal theorem-proof presentation.

gems: A ground/Hubble pair turns convolution into something visible: the broader ground point-spread function smears each point source, while the space telescope reveals much narrower optical blur. [Lecture 9, slides 2-4]

The damped oscillator's amplitude peak is not at either pole's imaginary part or at the undamped natural frequency: the geometry yields omega_peak^2=omega_d^2-sigma^2, while -pi/2 phase occurs at omega0. The live apparatus is simply ten Slinky loops, a bolt, and a motor-driven cam. [Lecture 9, slides 57-67; official transcript 00:12:42-00:14:29]

The perching case starts with a memorable scale disparity: average drag coefficients are 0.16 for a Boeing 747, 0.25 for the Cornell perching plane, and 10 for a common pigeon; matching the pigeon would require a cruising 747 to stop in about 40 meters. The course glider later reaches 1.1. [Lecture 10, slides 5 and 13; official transcript 00:03:38-00:05:23]

The controlled glider enters motion capture at 6 m/s, reaches a perch less than 3.5 m away, and completes the full trajectory in under one second. The guest lecturer adds that an open-loop command misses every time, while feedback hits the perch every time. [Lecture 10, slide 11; official transcript 00:07:12-00:08:27]

The ideal wallFinder reaches a target one meter away in one 0.1-second step by commanding exactly 10 m/s when KT=-1; the pole-at-zero result and physical motion agree perfectly. [Lecture 10, slides 22-29]

One sample of sensor delay changes the fastest possible pole from 0 to a repeated pole at 0.5; one more delay pushes it to about 0.682. The same robot makes delay's cost numerically undeniable. [Lecture 10, slides 50-53]

A first-order Bode magnitude asymptote misses the exact response by only about 3 dB at the corner and rapidly improves away from it, explaining why hand construction is useful rather than merely traditional. [Lecture 11, slide 38]

The high-Q pole geometry yields three compact design heuristics at once: peak gain approximately Q, normalized 3 dB bandwidth approximately 1/Q, and about pi/2 phase change across that narrow band. [Lecture 11, slides 43-63]
The LM741 example uses K0=200,000 but a dominant pole at only 40 rad/s (about 6.4 Hz); feedback converts that apparently poor audio amplifier into a gain-bandwidth lesson. [Lecture 12, slides 6-23]

Op-amp feedback speeds the response and extends bandwidth by 1+beta K0, yet the initial rate of voltage change does not increase—the faster result comes from accepting a smaller final value. [Lecture 12, slides 20-23]

Bach's G-minor violin sonata is played through a transistor crossover-distortion demo at gains 2, 4, 8, and 16, turning an abstract dead zone into an audible experiment; Freeman notes that practical acceptability would require loop gain nearer 1,000. [Lecture 13, slide 17; official transcript 00:17:11-00:19:38]

Magnetic levitation and a spring/mass have nearly identical block diagrams with one sign reversed; that sign rotates poles from the imaginary axis to the real axis and creates an unstable mode. [Lecture 13, slides 26-30]

A threefold zebra enlargement makes convolution's practical payoff visible: pixel replication produces jagged stripes, while the separable triangular filter yields fewer jagged edges. [Problem Set 5 Solution, Engineering Problem 5, pp. 9-12]

The smiley matched filter still finds the nose at column 765, row 432 when Gaussian noise has standard deviation 150—more than half the full black-to-white level difference. [Problem Set 5 Solution, Engineering Problem 6, pp. 13-15]

The suspension design has a counterintuitive bad extreme: with B=100, h(t) is nearly an impulse, so the stiff shock absorber transmits the wheel's bump directly to the passenger compartment and might as well not be there. [Problem Set 6 Solution, Engineering Problem 5, pp. 7-9]

The DTMF detector places poles at the desired 1209 Hz column tone after 10 kHz sampling; r between roughly 0.9 and 0.99 gives discrimination without unacceptable instability or lingering response. [Problem Set 6 Solution, Engineering Problem 6, pp. 9-12]

The same characteristic polynomial has a much wider CT stability range (K>2) than DT (2<K<3), a compact demonstration that 'left half-plane' and 'inside the unit circle' are materially different constraints. [Problem Set 6 Solution, Problems 3-4, pp. 5-6]

Hewlett and Packard's founding phase-shift-oscillator circuit becomes marginally stable at K=8; with 1 kohm and 1 microfarad sections its period is 3.63 ms, and a tenfold resistor change stretches it to 36.3 ms without changing critical gain. [Problem Set 7 Solution, Engineering Problem 3, pp. 5-6]

The robotic-steering design cleanly exposes controller roles: position feedback alone oscillates, derivative feedback alone leaves offset, and the combined controller can converge to the lane center with controlled damping. [Problem Set 7 Solution, Engineering Problem 4, pp. 6-9]

Quiz 2 opens with the noncausal-looking h(t)=exp(-|t|); its bilateral transform gives y-y''=2x, forcing students to separate an LTI input-output equation from a causal realization. [Quiz 2 Solution, Problem 1, p. 2]
